analysis.one_liner: Strips the President's power to pause or block new oil, gas, coal, and mining leases on federal land without Congress's approval.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Senate Energy Committee in January 2021 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The POWER Act would have required the President and federal agencies to get Congress's approval before doing anything that would stop or substantially delay new oil and gas, coal, hardrock mining, or critical minerals leases and permits on federal land — including national forests, public lands, and the outer continental shelf. It would also have barred the President from withdrawing federal land from mineral and geothermal development without a new act of Congress. In practice, this would have taken away the executive branch's existing power to pause fossil fuel leasing on public land and given that decision only to Congress. The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil, gas, coal, and mining companies that lease federal land would be the main beneficiaries: no president could pause or slow new leases and permits on federal land — including national forests, public lands, and offshore waters — without a new law from Congress, guaranteeing continued access to publicly owned resources. Communities and workers in fossil fuel producing regions would also benefit from continued leasing activity. Anyone who wanted stable, predictable federal energy supply without executive policy swings would gain.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil, gas, coal, and mining companies

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits the President or agencies from any action that would prohibit or substantially delay new oil and gas, coal, hardrock, or critical minerals leases, permits, or approvals on federal land unless Congress passes a law authorizing it.

It blocks the President from withdrawing federal lands from mineral and geothermal leasing, mining entry, or other development uses without an act of Congress, keeping lands currently open to extraction open.
It was a response to the new administration's early 2021 pauses on new oil and gas leasing on federal lands, locking current leasing levels in place across future administrations.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost through continued carbon emissions from expanded fossil fuel extraction on public land, loss of executive ability to protect public lands and waters from development, and forgone alternatives like parks, wildlife habitat, or recreation on land that could no longer be withdrawn from mining or leasing. Because hardrock mining under federal law pays no royalty, taxpayers would also forgo revenue while bearing the land and water impacts.

drawbacks.text: The bill would sharply limit the President's existing authority to protect public lands and waters, making it harder to pause oil, gas, coal, and hardrock mining activity on federal land even for conservation or climate reasons, and harder to reserve land for parks, wildlife habitat, or recreation.

By requiring an act of Congress for any pause, the bill would let a single chamber block federal energy decisions indefinitely, entrenching current levels of extraction on public land regardless of changing market or environmental conditions.

Supporters' stated concern — that abrupt leasing moratoria harm energy-producing communities and could raise prices — is a real cost of executive pauses, but this remedy would remove the ability to act at all rather than managing those transitions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have given oil, gas, coal, and mining companies a guarantee that federal land stays open to leasing regardless of which party holds the White House, which supporters argued protects energy jobs and supply. The cost is that Congress — not agencies with technical staff — would have the final say over routine leasing decisions, making it far harder to slow fossil fuel development on public lands for climate, conservation, or local-quality-of-life reasons, and harder to reserve land for parks, wildlife, or other uses. For most Americans, the environmental and public-land costs outweigh the guarantee of continued extraction.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Senate Energy Committee, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 28, 2021, read twice, and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, where its progress ended.
The action history shows no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, and no further action of any kind through the end of the 117th Congress in January 2023.
All 29 Senate supporters were Republicans, so the bill had no path in a Senate where 50 Republicans could not by themselves bring a bill to the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who use or value federal public lands are better off that the bill died, and so are anyone who favors keeping executive authority to restrict fossil fuel development on public land; no industry gained the guaranteed lease access it would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public-land users; no executive curbs on leasing

sides.party_line_note: All 29 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat or Independent supported it, and the bill died in committee without a vote.

industries.note: The bill would guarantee that new federal oil and gas leases and permits could not be paused or slowed by a president, keeping the federal leasing pipeline open. This removes the main lever an administration has to limit drilling on public land, which ordinary people bear as carbon emissions and lost public-land uses.

New federal coal leases could not be substantially delayed or stopped without Congress, locking in continued federal coal extraction. Coal combustion carries public health and climate costs that the bill would make harder to limit.

New hardrock leases, permits, and mining claims on federal land could not be restricted without Congress, and land could not be withdrawn from mining entry. Mining claims on federal land operate under 19th-century law with no federal royalty, so the public would keep bearing land and water impacts without a revenue offset.

The bill also protects new critical minerals leasing and geothermal leasing on federal land. Some critical-minerals development serves stated national goals like supply chains for batteries, but the bill would prevent any siting restrictions on that development, so the public trade-off is not managed.
